Japanese lexical norms: from stimulus items to documented matches

Source: vignettes/japanese-norms.Rmd
japanese-norms.Rmd

Suppose you are selecting Japanese words for a lexical-decision or reading experiment. You need to inspect each item’s normative ratings, how many people rated it, and which items have no match. Keep those rows and experimental conditions together before comparing groups. A document average alone cannot show that a particular stimulus was unmatched.

This guide uses existing lexdiv_norm_profile() calculations and an optional local-file example. No external norm values, participant data or dictionaries are bundled. The executable illustration uses invented values; sections using real data run only when you explicitly supply the separately obtained files. The example script can be loaded in R without a shell or Python.

Choose a construct and check the data terms

Resource Information Data terms and scope
WLSP-familiarity v4.0 Familiarity/use estimates for knowing, reading, writing, speaking and listening CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Local-file candidate review below; record choices remain explicit
WLSP-norms v1.0 Subjective polysemousness estimates CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. Reviewed record lookup and KWIC connection; values are not sense counts
AWD-J core Human abstractness ratings for 15,220 words CC BY 4.0. Scale-direction descriptions conflict; no automatic transformation here. EX contains model predictions
Japanese AoA Retrospective acquisition ratings for 5,736 words Data: CC BY-NC 4.0, independently of the article’s CC BY license. Local-file example below
JALEX Lexical-decision response times and accuracy The data’s license.txt specifies CC BY-NC 4.0. Current data version/exclusion rules need separate review
Japanese BOI Body-object interaction ratings OSF project: CC BY 4.0. Local-file example below; publication/file scope caveat applies

These conditions were checked on 2026-10-05. Free access does not by itself permit redistribution. Follow attribution and other applicable conditions for the actual data, including joined tables or extracts; this package’s MIT code license does not relicense imported data. An OSF project’s license does not automatically clear third-party columns in a merged table.

Familiarity, frequency, acquisition age, abstractness, BOI and reaction time measure different things. Do not average them into an undocumented difficulty score. Adult native-speaker ratings are not an individual Japanese learner’s acquisition history, known vocabulary, or ability to use a word appropriately.

Keep a row for every stimulus

Use item_id as the study’s unique identifier. A word can occur in several items or conditions: the lookup form need not be unique. term is the exact spelling to look up. Keep the displayed stimulus, reading, sense and any mapping decisions in additional columns if they differ from the lookup form.

items <- data.frame(
  item_id = c("a1", "a2", "b1", "b2", "b3"),
  condition = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "B"),
  term = c("学校", "研究", "学校", "辞書", "未登録の例語")
)

For a CSV, use read.csv("stimuli.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", colClasses = "character") when IDs must retain leading zeros. Convert numeric design variables separately. The real-data helper below rejects duplicate or missing IDs, missing lookup forms, and output-column collisions. It preserves input order and extra columns; it does not tokenize, normalize or resolve senses.

Inspect matches before interpreting averages

The following table is authored demonstration data, not Japanese norms. It includes a matched word with a missing annotation, as well as a query word absent from the table. Both produce NA, with different reasons.

toy <- data.frame(term = c("学校", "研究", "辞書"),
                  rating = c(2, 5, NA_real_))
specs <- data.frame(measure_id = "illustration", value_column = "rating",
  construct_id = "authored_illustration", value_unit = "invented_rating_points",
  direction = "descriptive", language = "Japanese", variety = "unspecified",
  population_id = "authored_not_participant_data", collection_year = "not_observed",
  valid_min = 1, valid_max = 7)
resource <- list(resource_id = "authored_ja_norms", resource_version = "1",
  creator = "Example author", source_reference = "Invented values in this guide",
  data_license = "MIT: authored illustration", transformation_id = "none",
  lookup_unit = "authored_spelling", resource_key_normalization_id = "identity-v1")
example <- lexdiv_norm_profile(items$term, toy, "term", specs, resource)
item_table <- cbind(items, example$lookup[, c("value", "lookup_status", "value_status")])
item_table
#>   item_id condition         term value       lookup_status       value_status
#> 1      a1         A         学校     2    matched_resource           observed
#> 2      a2         A         研究     5    matched_resource           observed
#> 3      b1         B         学校     2    matched_resource           observed
#> 4      b2         B         辞書    NA    matched_resource missing_annotation
#> 5      b3         B 未登録の例語    NA unknown_to_resource not_applicable_oov
example$summary[, c("weighting", "estimate", "resource_coverage",
                     "value_coverage", "annotation_coverage")]
#>   weighting estimate resource_coverage value_coverage annotation_coverage
#> 1     token      3.0              0.80            0.6           0.7500000
#> 2      type      3.5              0.75            0.5           0.6666667
stopifnot(identical(item_table$item_id, items$item_id),
          isTRUE(all.equal(example$summary$estimate, c(3, 3.5))))

For item-row (token) weighting, 4/5 rows match the resource, 3/5 have a value, and 3/4 matched rows have an annotation. The mean is (2 + 5 + 2) / 3 = 3. For distinct-spelling (type) weighting, the mean is (2 + 5) / 2 = 3.5. Here “token” means each supplied item row, not an independently observed corpus token. Neither mean should replace item-level information in the experiment.

Inspect missingness by condition rather than silently dropping unmatched rows:

condition_coverage <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(item_table, item_table$condition),
  function(x) data.frame(condition = x$condition[1], items = nrow(x),
    with_value = sum(x$value_status == "observed"),
    without_value = sum(x$value_status != "observed"),
    value_coverage = mean(x$value_status == "observed"))))
rownames(condition_coverage) <- NULL
condition_coverage
#>   condition items with_value without_value value_coverage
#> 1         A     2          2             0      1.0000000
#> 2         B     3          1             2      0.3333333

In this illustration, condition A has values for both items, whereas B has values for only one of three. A comparison of available-value means would use different subsets. Review the unmatched forms and selection rules before interpreting such a comparison. Do not equate missing values with zero, rarity, low familiarity, or lack of participant knowledge.

Use a separately obtained AoA or BOI file

Download data_AoA.csv from the AoA project or data_boi.csv from the BOI project after checking the terms for your intended use. Each can be used independently. Use the aggregate file, not raw participant responses or a merged collection of third-party norms.

The helper checks the inspected file’s SHA-256; a changed file fails rather than silently acquiring the old metadata. Both inspected files contain 5,736 unique Word keys. A future version requires reviewing the source and updating the example, not disabling the hash check without examining the change.

source(system.file("examples", "japanese-norms.R", package = "ldfreq"))
aoa <- profile_japanese_norm_items(items, "data_AoA.csv", resource = "aoa")
aoa$items                  # Original IDs/conditions plus source IDs, n, SD and values
aoa$profile$coverage        # Resource, value and annotation coverage
aoa$source                 # Citation, data license, input hash and limitation

# Independent alternative: obtaining AoA is not required to use BOI.
boi <- profile_japanese_norm_items(items, "data_boi.csv", resource = "boi")

AoA norm_mean is the mean of seven age-category ratings, not years. Categories run from 1 (0–1 years) to 7 (12+ years); the instructions also assign unknown acquisition age to 7. The aggregate cannot separate those responses. See Mochizuki & Ota (2025).

BOI norm_mean is the original mean rating. The 2026 publication and OSF project title say 5,637 words, whereas the inspected CSV and analysis script contain 5,736. The content of the correction has not been verified here. Treat this as a reproducible lookup into the pinned file, not replication of the corrected publication’s analysis sample.

norm_n and norm_sd describe the source ratings, not the sample size or uncertainty of your own experiment. A normative SD is not a standard error for a condition difference. Preserve source sampling, repeated participants/items, and your experiment’s task when choosing a statistical model.

Join resources and save the record

Join by the study item ID, after separately matching each resource’s spelling. Do not assume that two data providers’ numerical source IDs are equal. Do not use an inner join that discards unmatched stimuli.

index <- match(aoa$items$item_id, boi$items$item_id)
stopifnot(!anyNA(index), !anyDuplicated(boi$items$item_id))
combined <- aoa$items
combined$boi_mean <- boi$items$norm_mean[index]
combined$boi_value_status <- boi$items$norm_value_status[index]
# Source details for both resources stay in the RDS, alongside the flat table.
saveRDS(list(aoa = aoa, boi = boi, combined = combined,
             session = sessionInfo()), "japanese-norm-analysis.rds")
write.csv(combined, "japanese-norm-items.csv", row.names = FALSE,
          fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
restored <- readRDS("japanese-norm-analysis.rds")
stopifnot(identical(restored$combined, combined))

Why spelling alone sometimes fails

WLSP includes multiple readings for spellings such as 人気 (にんき and ひとけ). Even spelling plus reading is not necessarily unique in the inspected file: 上手 includes repeated じょうず records with different estimates. Inspect the original record IDs, headings, reading and classification before defining a correspondence. The generic profile deliberately rejects duplicate keys; it does not pick the first row or average distinct entries automatically.

Keep a separate, explicit correspondence table when a study item needs a particular source record. Review each mapping in context. A morphological analyzer’s lemma is not evidence of a uniquely correct psycholinguistic norm match. For running text, start with the Japanese annotation workflow and retain source positions, forms, dictionary and segmentation decisions.

Review WLSP candidates and record your choices

The bundled wlsp-items.R example reads a separately obtained bunruidb-fam.csv from WLSP-familiarity v4.0, with its verified file hash. It returns every exact-spelling candidate, retaining record ID, heading, reading, classification, record type and the five published estimates for knowing, writing, reading, speaking and listening. Numeric estimates are not converted into probabilities, raw rating points or individual knowledge scores. The data remain subject to CC BY-NC-SA 3.0; no WLSP ratings are bundled.

For occurrences in running text, the KWIC review guide uses the same local-file reader through wlsp_ambiguity_candidates() to retain record IDs, readings and classifications as contextual review candidates. It also shows how to compare two reviewers while keeping unresolved cases.

The following are authored study items. The reading and context specify the intended stimulus; the helper keeps them as metadata and does not use them to automatically discard candidates or resolve word senses.

source(system.file("examples", "wlsp-items.R", package = "ldfreq"))
stimuli <- data.frame(
  item_id = c("p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5"),
  condition = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "B"),
  term = c("人気", "人気", "学校", "上手", "未登録の例語"),
  intended_reading = c("にんき", "ひとけ", "がっこう", "じょうず", NA),
  context = c("この商品は人気がある。", "夜の公園には人気がない。",
              "学校に通う。", "彼は料理が上手だ。", "作成した未照合例。")
)
path <- "bunruidb-fam.csv"
review <- review_wlsp_items(stimuli, path)
review$items[, c("item_id", "term", "wlsp_candidate_count", "wlsp_status")]
review$candidates[, c("item_id", "record_id", "heading", "reading",
                     "classification", "classification_label", "know")]

For this pinned file the candidate counts are 2, 2, 1, 7 and 0. None is selected automatically, including the single candidate for 学校. The five study rows remain separate from the twelve candidate rows. Candidate multiplicity must not increase an item’s weight in subsequent analyses.

After inspecting the candidates, record one source record per chosen item and a reason. This example selects the two intended readings of 人気 and the reviewed 学校 entry. It leaves 上手 unresolved: reading alone does not make its correspondence unique.

chosen <- subset(review$candidates,
  (item_id == "p1" & reading == "にんき") |
  (item_id == "p2" & reading == "ひとけ") | item_id == "p3")
stopifnot(nrow(chosen) == 3L,
          identical(chosen$item_id, c("p1", "p2", "p3")))
decisions <- data.frame(
  item_id = chosen$item_id, record_id = chosen$record_id,
  reason = c("Reviewed heading/reading for the intended popularity stimulus",
             "Reviewed heading/reading for the intended human-presence stimulus",
             "Reviewed the single school entry against the stimulus")
)
resolved <- review_wlsp_items(stimuli, path, decisions)
resolved$items[, c("item_id", "wlsp_status", "wlsp_record_id",
                   "wlsp_reason", "wlsp_know")]

selected records an explicit correspondence, unreviewed means candidates exist but none was chosen, and unmatched means no exact-spelling candidate exists. Unselected values stay NA; so do missing values in a selected source record. Inspect selection status and the value you intend to analyze. The helper rejects unknown item/record IDs, multiple choices for one item, blank reasons, choices whose source spelling differs from the item, and files that differ from the inspected snapshot. It does not validate a reviewer’s linguistic judgment. Repeated spellings across different item IDs are allowed.

Do not read these decisions as validated sense-specific familiarity norms. The upstream description says that estimation changed to surface forms from version 3, yet the inspected table still contains different estimates for some repeated heading/reading combinations. A recorded mapping makes the choice auditable; it does not settle that methodological issue. Uncertain mappings can remain unresolved or be compared in explicitly labeled sensitivity analyses.

Keep the denominator and reasons visible, including items without values:

selection_coverage <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(resolved$items, resolved$items$condition), function(x) data.frame(
    condition = x$condition[1], items = nrow(x),
    with_candidates = sum(x$wlsp_candidate_count > 0),
    selected = sum(x$wlsp_status == "selected"),
    with_know_value = sum(!is.na(x$wlsp_know)))))
selection_coverage
write.csv(decisions, "wlsp-decisions.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
# Source record IDs such as 002375 have leading zeros: preserve them as text.
saved_decisions <- read.csv("wlsp-decisions.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8",
                           colClasses = "character")
restored <- review_wlsp_items(stimuli, path, saved_decisions)
stopifnot(identical(restored$items, resolved$items))
saveRDS(list(review = resolved, coverage = selection_coverage,
             session = sessionInfo()), "wlsp-item-review.rds")

Report which of the five estimates you used and why. The helper returns item-level values without pooling across candidate records or experimental conditions. In this example, condition A has two chosen items with values and B has one of three: report the remaining unreviewed and unmatched items before interpreting condition means. The example caps expansion at one million candidate pairs; review smaller item sets if needed.

Report what the analysis can answer

Record the resource/file version, population, scale, lookup form and any mapping or exclusion rule. Report coverage for each condition and the subset used for each comparison. Examine distributions as well as averages when selecting stimuli; similar means alone do not establish balanced conditions.

This workflow documents normative features of the chosen items. It does not validate a proficiency score, diagnose knowledge from an unmatched word, or establish causal effects of familiarity or acquisition age on response time. For corpus-level profiles, see multiple-document norms. To combine these sources with Japanese TUBELEX, review item-level missingness and inspect condition distributions, follow the stimulus-selection workflow.
